extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/history of science and scientists interested in scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for discovering and testing scientific laws by induction, experiment, and deduction (as discussed in editorial notes on Bacon). Emphasizes types of instances, experimental design, mathematical completion of induction, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective instances are general facts or laws of some degree of generality that are themselves the result of induction (e.g., the system of Jupiter or Saturn with satellites assisting the admission of the Copernican system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregated systems or sets of phenomena that display the pattern of interest in miniature to support induction. Examples given: planetary systems supporting heliocentrism; Kepler's laws as collective instances that opened the way to Newtonian gravitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ocular collective instances (many-part phenomena shown at once)
rubrics_metrics.description: A species of collective instance in which particular phenomena are presented in such numbers at once that the induction of their law becomes a matter of ocular inspection (e.g., the parabolic form of a water jet, figures produced by sand on vibrating plates, colored lemniscates in polarized light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many individual elements are seen together they can make the general law immediately apparent; such displays function as heuristic 'advanced posts' in exploration and rapidly suggest the mathematical expression of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crucial instances (decisive experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucial instances are experiments or facts that most readily and securely eliminate extraneous causes and decide between rival hypotheses, especially when the rival theories lead to different consequences on a single fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that produce different observable outcomes depending on which theory is correct (example: Fresnel's test with two glass plates and a prism producing alternating dark and bright stripes under different theoretical expectations). Crucial instances are prized for adjudicating between competing explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontier and itinerant instances (law of continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontier and itinerant instances are cases that trace the general law of continuity pervading nature (natura non agit per saltum), showing intermediate forms between extremes (e.g., gold-leaf transparency as a frontier between transparent and opaque).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek phenomena that occupy boundary positions between categories to expose gradual transitions and continuity; these help reveal that opposed qualities may be degrees of the same property rather than strict opposites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false exclusions and defective enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining an effect by enumerating and excluding possible causes (dilemma/elimination), one must guard against falsely excluding genuine causes or failing to enumerate all relevant causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude by simple elimination unless the list of alternative causes is exhaustive and exclusions valid; the text cites Bacon's omissions in tidal theory (ignoring polar ice melting and thermal expansion) as an example of defective enumeration and false exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematics/geometry to complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When experiment determines particular values but a constant relation is suspected between quantities, geometry or mathematical deduction is necessary to discover the general rule (e.g., deriving the cosine law in refraction or Newton explaining the rainbow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call in mathematical/deductive methods to infer general relations from sets of measured instances; induction plus geometry can produce infallible or approximate general laws where experiment alone cannot provide the general formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise measurement and quantitative observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of certain laws (e.g., gravitation) requires accurate geometrical measures and quantitative data (demi-diameter of the earth, velocity of falling bodies, distance of the moon, orbital speed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize precise, quantitative experiments and measurements; many theoretical laws cannot be discovered or confirmed without accurate quantification and comparability of experimental data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments and experiments to reveal non-sensory facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus such as the air-pump, barometer, measurements of the velocity of light, experiments in electricity and galvanism, and pneumatic chemistry elicit scientific facts that unaided sense perception cannot reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ appropriate instruments and controlled experimental setups to uncover phenomena beyond direct sensory detection; such tools expand the scope of empirical discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between natural and artificial productions as heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies between natural and artificial contrivances (e.g., hydraulic engine valves and blood-vessel contrivances) can be fruitful guides to discovery (Harvey's circulation example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-founded analogical reasoning to suggest mechanisms or experiments, but treat analogy as heuristic rather than conclusive proof; verify analogical hypotheses by observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of syllogistic assumptions and paralogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are one form of reasoning, but assumptions about middle-term transitivity or uniform relations can be misleading (relations between terms may differ in kind); reasoning by dilemma is liable to paralogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply logical forms carefully, checking that relations are preserved across terms and avoiding fallacious exclusions or hidden shifts in meaning; explicitly test logical assumptions against empirical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dichotomy to strengthen dilemmas (Ramus's approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing divisions to two contradictory propositions (dichotomy) was proposed to make reasoning by dilemma and crucial instances more certain by ensuring one of two contradictory alternatives must hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, structure investigative divisions into clear contradictory pairs to increase decisiveness, but ensure that the dichotomy legitimately partitions the possibility space and does not mask intermediate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize both practical and theoretical import of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments may be considered merely for practical ends or for their theoretical importance; some classes of experiments have greater theoretical value in establishing universal laws (e.g., gravitation needed diverse precise observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate experiments both for immediate practical utility and for their capacity to contribute to theory-building; do not relegate experiments to mere practice when they may yield fundamental theoretical insight.
